q: We introduced Vibe Code Bench, a benchmark of 100 web application specifications evaluated through 964 browser-based workflows.
r: Include: new benchmark for end-to-end web application development from specifications, with cost and variance analysis.

q: We model the operational cost of resolving a software-engineering task as the number of input and output tokens an AI coding agent would consume
r: EC6: SWE-bench-repository commit-level cost model (task resolution as in SWE-bench), modelled not run, so issue-repair style and not feature/project level.

q: This study investigated the structural quality of AI-generated software, moving beyond functional correctness to audit the technical debt introduced by both single LLMs and autonomous multi-agent systems.
r: Include: empirical quality (code and architectural smell) evaluation of agents generating complete multi-file projects with MetaGPT.

q: We measured two of the most popular ones on real multi-turn sessions, installed the way a user installs them, with a correctness gate on every run
r: Include: cost-aware, correctness-gated evaluation method with repeated trials for skills/plugins used inside a coding agent; contribution is the evaluation method.

q: We evaluate three coding agents, Claude Code [2], OpenAI Codex [20], and Gemini Code Assist [6], across 300 generated artifacts spanning Python, JavaScript, and Java.
r: Include: controlled comparison of three coding agents generating complete applications from standardized prompts, with an execution-reliability metric.

q: Across thirteen models evaluated under a single agent harness, even the strongest often pass visible tests but fail withheld variants
r: Include: new repository-level benchmark where agents implement executable Gherkin specifications across a lifecycle, with repeated runs.

q: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in Software Engineering (SWE), yet evaluating their performance on realistic project-level SWE remains challenging.
r: Include: new project-level benchmark for agents with user-simulated end-to-end evaluation.

q: NITR is ultimately a step toward a broader shift in how we evaluate LLM for software engineering: from asking whether models can produce correct code, to asking whether they can participate responsibly
r: Include: published ASE'26 version (rayyan-800486182 is the preprint, EC4 there); new maintainability benchmark with dual oracles for repository edits by agents.

q: This paper presents an example of the design process of a singleshot vibe-coded LSC tool for a given lifelog data layer.
r: EC6: case study building one tool in a single specialised domain (lifelog retrieval); contribution is the tool design, not the evaluation method.

q: This survey follows a widely-used systematic literature review (SLR) methodology
r: Include: systematic survey of AI coding agents (secondary study with a described search); reviews are kept.
